# Volume 4 — CHAPTER 18 SPRING DAYS

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

The March suns caused the harbor ice to turn black and decay; blue waters and a breezy, white-crested gulf returned in April; and the light of Seven Gulls once more adorned the twilights like jewels.
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0000 }

“It brings me such joy to view it again,” Nell remarked, during the initial night that it returned. “During the entire winter, I felt its absence deeply. Without its presence, the sky to the northwest has appeared empty and desolate.”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0001 }

Extremely young, golden-green foliage imparted a softness to the countryside. Over the trees past the Glen hung a haze of emerald. During the early morning, enchanted vapors filled the glens facing the sea.
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0002 }

Energetic breezes blew back and forth, carrying the spray of salty foam upon their breath. Resembling an attractive, flirty female, the ocean giggled, sparkled, groomed itself, and enticed. Schools of herring gathered, causing the fishing community to rouse itself into activity. White sails heading toward the channel filled the harbor with vitality. Vessels started journeying out to sea and returning back again.
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0003 }

“During a spring day such as this,” Nell remarked, “I am certain of the precise feeling my soul will experience on the morning of resurrection.”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0004 }

“Occasionally during spring, I kind of get the impression that I could have turned into a poet had I been trained early,” Captain Saul observed. “I discover that I am reviewing ancient rhymes and lines I listened to the schoolmaster declaiming six decades back. During different seasons, they do not bother me. At present, I feel driven to go forth onto the stones or the meadows or the sea and recite them aloud.”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0005 }

It was during that afternoon that Captain Saul arrived, delivering to Nell some sweet-grass he had gathered while wandering across the sand dunes, along with a quantity of shells intended for her garden.
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0006 }

“It’s becoming truly rare beside this beach these days,” he remarked. “During my childhood there was an abundance of it. However, nowadays you will merely discover a patch occasionally—and at no time when you are searching for it. You simply must chance upon it—you are strolling across the sand dunes, not at all considering sweet-grass—and suddenly a sweet fragrance fills the atmosphere—and the grass is right beneath your steps. I prefer the scent of sweet-grass. It constantly brings my mother to my mind.”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0007 }

“Was she attached to it?” Nell inquired.
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0008 }

“Not as far as I am aware. I am not sure she ever encountered any sweet-grass. Rather, it is owing to its sort of maternal fragrance—not excessively youthful, you see—something rather mature, healthy, and reliable—exactly like a mother. The schoolmaster’s bride perpetually stored it in her handkerchief drawer. You could place that small bundle with your own, Mistress Carrow. Store-bought perfumes are not to my liking—yet a hint of sweet-grass fits in any place a lady inhabits.”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0009 }

Nell had felt no great excitement about the prospect of bordering her flower beds using quahog shells; as an embellishment, they failed to attract her initially. However, she refused to wound Captain Saul’s emotions under any circumstances; consequently, she feigned an appreciation she initially lacked, expressing warm gratitude to him. Then, after Captain Saul had boastfully bordered each bed using a ring formed from the large, milk-white shells, Nell discovered, much to her astonishment, that the result pleased her. Upon a lawn in town, or even higher up at the Glen, such things would have felt out of place, yet right here, within the traditional, ocean-bordered garden belonging to the small house of dreams, they BELONGED.
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0010 }

“They TRULY appear lovely,” she remarked with genuine feeling.
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0011 }

“Cowhawks were constantly encircling her flowerbeds, the schoolmaster’s bride’s,” Captain Saul remarked. “Flowers were her true specialty. Her mere LOOK—and touch—LIKE THAT—made them grow at a wild pace. Certain people possess that talent—and I believe you possess it as well, Mistress Carrow.”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0012 }

“Oh, I am not sure—yet I adore my garden, and working in it brings me great joy. To putter around with green, growing vegetation, observing daily to witness the precious, fresh shoots emerge, feels like assisting in creation, in my opinion. At this moment my garden resembles faith—the evidence of things unseen. But wait a little.”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0013 }

“Observing those small, shriveled brown seeds and contemplating the rainbows inside them never fails to astonish me,” Captain Saul stated. “As I reflect upon those seeds, believing that our souls will endure in different realms becomes not in the least bit difficult for me. Had you not witnessed the wonder yourself, you could scarcely accept that vitality existed within those minuscule objects—some no larger than specks of dust—to say nothing of fragrance and hue, could you?”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0014 }

Nell, who was reckoning her remaining days like the silver beads of a rosary, had become unable to make the long journey to the lighthouse or along the Glen road. Nevertheless, Captain Saul and Miss Winifred visited the small house frequently. The delight of Hugh’s and Nell’s lives was Miss Winifred. Following each visit, her remarks caused them to laugh uproariously. Great amusement was provided to anyone listening whenever she and Captain Saul chanced to be at the small house together. A battle of words occurred between them, wherein she launched attacks and he maintained a defense. Nell on one occasion chided the Captain because he baited Miss Winifred.
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0015 }

“Oh, I truly delight in getting her started, Mistress Carrow,” laughed the shameless offender. “Nothing in my existence brings me more entertainment. That tongue she possesses could scorch a rock. And both you and that youthful rascal of a physician derive just as much pleasure from hearing her as I do.”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0016 }

Captain Saul arrived on a different evening so that he could give Nell a handful of mayflowers. The moist, fragrant air of a spring evening by the sea filled the garden. A white mist like milk lingered at the border of the ocean, touched by the light of a new moon, while stars shone with silver joy above the Glen. The bell from the church on the opposite side of the harbor rang with a dreamy sweetness. Through the twilight, that rich ringing drifted until it combined with the sea's gentle spring murmur. The night's enchantment received its final, perfecting element from Captain Saul’s mayflowers.
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0017 }

“I haven’t noticed any this spring, and I’ve missed them,” said Nell, pressing her face into them.
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0018 }

“They cannot be located near Seven Gulls, but solely within the barrens back behind the Glen up there. I made a short journey today unto the Land-of-nothing-to-do, and searched these out on your behalf. I suppose they are the final ones you will behold this spring, because they are almost finished.”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0019 }

“You are so considerate and generous, Captain Saul. No one beside you—not even Hugh”—shaking her head toward him—“recalled my constant spring yearning for mayflowers.”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0020 }

“Furthermore, I had an additional task—I wished to bring a meal of trout back over there to Mr. Stroud. He enjoys one now and then, and doing this is the sole way I can repay him for a favor he previously did me. Remaining there the entire afternoon, I conversed with him. He enjoys conversing with me, despite the fact that he is a very educated man whereas I am merely an uneducated old sailor, since he belongs to that class of people who MUST converse or else suffer misery, and he discovers that listeners are rare in this area. The people of The Glen keep their distance from him owing to their belief that he is an infidel. He is not quite that far gone—I suppose few men are—yet he could be described as a heretic. Heretics are evil, but they are extremely interesting. It is simply that they have become somewhat lost while searching for God, laboring under the belief that He is difficult to locate—which He never is. I suppose most of them stumble their way to Him eventually. I do not suppose that hearing Mr. Stroud’s reasoning is apt to cause me great injury. Mind you, my belief remains what I was taught from childhood to believe. It prevents a great deal of trouble—and beneath everything, God is good. The problem concerning Mr. Stroud is his being just a bit TOO smart. He believes he must act according to his smartness, and that finding a novel path to reach heaven is cleverer than following the ancient route that ordinary, uneducated people travel. However, he will arrive there eventually without doubt, and at that point he will mock his own foolishness.”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0021 }

“Mr. Stroud started out as a Methodist,” declared Miss Winifred, implying that moving from there to heresy was not a large step for him.
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0022 }

“Winifred, do you know,” Captain Saul remarked with seriousness, “I’ve frequently considered that were I not a Presbyterian, I would belong to the Methodists.”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0023 }

“Oh, all right,” Miss Winifred admitted, “if being a Presbyterian wasn't what you were, the rest wouldn't be of much importance. Talking about false doctrine brings to my mind, doctor—I returned the volume you borrowed me—that Natural Law in the Spiritual World—I only managed about a third. Sense is something I can read, and nonsense is something I can read, but neither description fits that work.”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0024 }

“It IS viewed as somewhat heretical by certain people,” Hugh conceded, “however I mentioned that to you prior to your taking it, Miss Winifred.”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0025 }

“Oh, I wouldn’t have cared about it being heretical. Wickedness is something I can endure, whereas foolishness is something I cannot,” Miss Winifred remarked placidly, giving off the impression that nothing more could possibly be uttered regarding Natural Law.
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0026 }

“On the topic of books, A Mad Love finally finished two weeks back,” Captain Saul observed thoughtfully. “One hundred and three chapters were in it. Once their wedding happened the book ceased immediately, meaning I suppose there were no more troubles for them. Isn’t it truly lovely that things happen like that in books at least, even though nowhere else is that the case?”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0027 }

“Novels are something I never read,” Miss Winifred remarked. “Captain Saul, have you heard any news about Geordie Russell’s condition today?”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0028 }

“Yes, I stopped by to visit him as I was heading home. He is recovering well—though he remains mired in a mess of problems, as always, poor chap.
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0029 }

“Granted, he makes the majority of it for his own consumption, yet I imagine that hardly renders it simpler to endure.”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0030 }

“Miss Winifred remarked that he was a terrible pessimist.”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0031 }

“Well, no, he isn’t precisely a pessimist, Winifred. He merely just does not ever discover a single thing that satisfies him.”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0032 }

“And does that not make one a pessimist?”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0033 }

“No, no. A pessimist is someone who does not ever anticipate discovering something that pleases him. Geordie has not reached THAT point yet.”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0034 }

“You’d discover a favorable word for Satan himself, Saul Garrick.”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0035 }

“Well, the tale of the elderly woman who called him persistent has reached your ears. However, Winifred, I possess no favorable words regarding the devil,” no.
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0036 }

“Have you any belief in him whatsoever?” inquired Miss Winifred with gravity.
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0037 }

“In what way can you inquire about that, Winifred, given your knowledge of my strong Presbyterian faith? In what manner would a Presbyterian manage if there were no devil?”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0038 }

“DO you?” Miss Winifred persisted.
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0039 }

SAUL, the Captain, was abruptly overcome by a serious demeanor.
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0040 }

“I put my faith in what a minister I once listened to termed 'a mighty and malignant and INTELLIGENT power of evil working in the universe,’” he declared with gravity. “I certainly do THAT, Winifred. You may label it the devil, or the 'principle of evil,’ or the Old Scratch, or whichever title pleases you. It EXISTS, and every single infidel and heretic on earth is unable to reason it out of existence, just as they are unable to reason God out of existence. It exists, and it is at work. However, mark my words, Winifred, I am convinced that it will ultimately be defeated.”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0041 }

“I certainly wish it to be the case,” Miss Winifred remarked with little optimism. “Yet regarding the devil, I feel certain he currently controls Barney Booth. Did you learn about Barney’s most recent behavior?”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0042 }

“No, what was it?”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0043 }

“Because he claims the men gazed at her with excessive admiration during her initial time wearing it to church, he went ahead and destroyed his wife’s brand-new, brown broadcloth suit, which set her back twenty-five dollars in Port Marlow. Isn’t that just how a man behaves?”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0044 }

“Mistress Booth IS very attractive, and brown suits her,” Captain Saul said thoughtfully.
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0045 }

“Does that justify him shoving her new suit inside the kitchen stove? Barney Booth is an envious idiot, and he renders his wife’s existence unhappy. She has wept the entire week over her suit. Oh, Nell, I wish I possessed your writing ability, believe ME. Wouldn’t I criticize a few of the men around here!”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0046 }

“Every one of those Booths is a bit peculiar,” Captain Saul remarked. “Barney appeared to be the most rational among them until he took a wife, at which point this strange possessive tendency surfaced in his character. As for his brother Daniel, he was perpetually strange.”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0047 }

“He threw fits every couple of days or thereabouts and refused to leave his bed,” Miss Winifred remarked with delight. “All the farm chores fell on his wife until his fit passed. People sent her notes of sympathy after his death; had I composed a message, it would have offered congratulations instead. Old Abram Booth, their father, was a vile old drunkard. At his wife’s burial, he was intoxicated, staggering around and hiccuping 'I didn’t dri—i—i—nk much but I feel a—a—awfully que—e—e—r.’ Upon his approaching me, I poked him hard in the back using my umbrella, which brought him to his senses until the casket was removed from the home. Yesterday was supposed to be young Johnny Booth’s wedding day, yet the ceremony could not happen since he went and caught the mumps. Is that not just like a man?”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0048 }

“Poor guy, in what way was he able to avoid contracting the mumps?”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0049 }

“Were I Kate Sterns, trust ME, I would not be feeling sorry for him. While I am uncertain how he could have avoided catching the mumps, I am CERTAIN that the wedding feast was fully made and that every bit of food will go bad prior to his recovery. What a loss! His time to have the mumps was during his childhood.”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0050 }

“Come along, Winifred, aren't you being a bit unreasonable, do you think?”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0051 }

Without deigning to answer, Miss Winifred addressed Tabitha Pratt instead, a stern-visaged, good-natured aged unwed woman from the Glen, who had been employed for a few weeks as a general servant at the small residence. Having gone to the Glen to visit an ill person, Tabitha had only recently come back.
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0052 }

“In what state is poor old Aunt Mandy this evening?” inquired Miss Winifred.
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0053 }

A sigh escaped Tabitha.
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0054 }

“Extremely ill—extremely ill, Winifred. I fear that she will shortly be in heaven, poor creature!”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0055 }

“Oh, certainly, things aren't quite that terrible!” Miss Winifred cried out in a sympathetic manner.
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0056 }

Captain Saul and Hugh exchanged glances. After that, they abruptly stood up and departed.
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0057 }

“There are moments,” Captain Saul remarked, amid fits, “in which refraining from laughter would be a sin. Those two fine ladies!”
{: #nw-v04-c18-p0058 }
